exp_mews_squad_blurb: Led a cross-functional squad responsible for the user experience across all Mews products. We took over the shells of every product, unifying and standardising them, along with the Dashboard of the main application, the PMS, and parts of the Smart Assistant Search engine. Designed and built the app switcher for the whole Mews ecosystem, end to end. Also took on backend maintenance over assets and translations. Planned the work and mentored junior engineers.
exp_mews_techlead_title: Tech Lead — Mews Design System, Platform team
exp_mews_techlead_blurb: On top of my senior engineer role, I took on the technical lead of the Mews Design System, as formal code owner of its libraries: the legacy library and the new implementations for both B2B and B2C. Among many other initiatives, I was responsible for, and the main contributor to, the work that followed an independent accessibility audit of Mews's guest-facing products against WCAG 2.1 AA and the European Accessibility Act — with the design system as one of its largest areas. Beyond that, I worked on large, key new components such as the DataGrid, built on TanStack Table and taken a long way past it: client-side, server-side and tree variants behind one API, and many user-facing features.
exp_mews_senior_title: Senior Software Engineer — Mews Design System, Platform team
exp_mews_senior_blurb: Shipped component libraries and frontend tooling for a large React/TypeScript monorepo, as the main contributor on my team and one of the top contributors to the whole repository. Likewise one of the main contributors to the multi-brand design-tokens pipeline (Figma → Token Studio → Style Dictionary), where one source of truth drives four themes across two brands on web and Android.
exp_liferay_blurb: Product engineer on the Tango team, working in Java and React through Liferay's portlets. I worked mostly on the Content Dashboard — audit charts, the item info panel, previews, versions, sharing and subscriptions — and on the Frontend Data Set, the tables shared across the platform; besides, prioritised segment variations for Collections, down to the Service Builder layer, and the Page Audit built on Google PageSpeed.
exp_docline_blurb: Led the frontend of a telemedicine platform, taking its Vue codebase to the next level — component reusability, best practices, and large-scale refactors, including introducing an app-wide shared store as the single source of truth for application state. Reviewed architecture, standardised code reviews, fostered a strong team culture, and improved the existing design system across Vue, TS and SCSS.
exp_indra_po_title: Product Owner & Engineer — Onesait platform website
exp_indra_po_blurb: Owned and delivered the main web app promoting Onesait products, bridging engineering and marketing. Led a team of four engineers and one designer, managing multiple stakeholders.
exp_indra_consultant_title: Senior Software Engineer & Consultant — Onesait Design System
exp_indra_consultant_blurb: Main delivery engineer on the Vue.js-based design system, and the go-to reference supporting every product engineering team adopting it.
exp_ironhack_blurb: Taught intensive full-stack web development bootcamps. Fast-paced and hands-on — and nothing hones your own fundamentals quite like teaching them to others.
exp_tau_blurb: Led a team of up to six developers at a design-led agency — client-facing work, pitching, and mentoring juniors — delivering marketing and corporate sites, e-commerce stores, and a steady stream of microsites for clients like Edelvives, ECAM, Universidad Autónoma, Mapfre and Telefónica. In a studio that lived and breathed design, the bar was pixel-perfect: high-craft UI, rich interactions, and truly responsive layouts, on jQuery, Bootstrap, PHP and WordPress, with Less and Sass built on Node, and our first steps in Angular.
exp_aulacm_blurb: Helped build and maintain the company's main site and the client websites delivered by its agency arm — my first taste of agency work and shipping custom WordPress in PHP. Doubled as the in-house WordPress instructor, teaching plugins, themes, styling and the PHP basics that make it all tick — and learning plenty the honest way myself.
exp_prev_blurb: A parallel life in sound, from around 2002 — production and post for film and TV. Two Goyas for documentaries, a Berlinale run after three weeks filming with orphans in Kenya, and a good showing at festivals besides; behind the desk, a Pro Tools wizard and Final Cut obsessive fluent in Avalon compressors, Neve preamps and a wall of top-notch mics. With my friend Iván I built lacasaestudio — still alive and thriving — and the instincts stuck: precision, grace under live pressure, reading a room, and tight teamwork.

cs_billing_intro: A billing engine that repays cash advances by taking a share of a merchant's daily revenue, driven day by day against a live API across a simulated month. It began as a take-home exercise, which is why the source stays private — I'm happy to walk anyone through it.
cs_billing_n1_h: One backlog, not three code paths
cs_billing_n1_b: Revenue that arrives late, a daily charge cap, and a charge the processor rejects look like three problems. They are one: an amount that could not settle today. Each advance carries a backlog, all three feed it, and the next day drains it under the same rules. The hard part of the brief turned out to be small once it had the right name.
cs_billing_n2_b: Amounts arrive as two-decimal strings, parsed once at the edge into a branded integer type and formatted once on the way out. The arithmetic in between goes through helpers that re-validate, so a float can never reach a balance. Rounding happens in exactly one place, and is documented because the spec was silent on it.
cs_billing_n3_h: A port, so every edge case is provable
cs_billing_n3_b: A live API cannot be asked to reject a charge or withhold a day's revenue on demand. One interface with two implementations — the real client and an in-memory fake — turns each failure mode into a deterministic test. All 136 of them run offline, in seconds.
cs_billing_n4_h: Decisions written down where the spec was silent
cs_billing_n4_b: Rounding, the accrual window, what becomes of an advance that cannot repay before the period ends, whether the daily cap is per advance or per mandate: each chosen once, pinned by a test, and listed with its reasoning. An architecture decision record covers the alternatives rejected — including the monorepo that would have demonstrated more and proved less.
cs_billing_shot1_alt: The run report: outstanding portfolio balance, collection statistics and every advance in the run.
cs_billing_shot1_cap: Each run writes a self-contained HTML report — no server, no build step, opens from disk.
cs_billing_shot2_alt: One advance's event ledger, showing eight consecutive rejected charges.
cs_billing_shot2_cap: An advance whose mandate stopped working. The balance stays intact and a human gets told; “stalled” is a reporting diagnosis, never a state the domain invents.
proj_billing_desc: A daily billing engine for cash advances: a pure domain core behind a ports-and-adapters seam, with late revenue, daily caps and rejected charges all carried forward by one mechanism.
proj_perico_desc: Rewrites plain Spanish in the voice of a cycling commentator — a RAG pipeline in Python, with FastAPI, pgvector and Claude.
cs_ensayadero_tagline: A rehearsal room that listens back.
cs_ensayadero_intro: A rehearsal tool for bands: upload a recording and get it back split into stems, with MIDI and an editable chord chart, in a multi-track mixer. In invite-only beta.
cs_ensayadero_n1_h: Self-hosted audio ML, no paid APIs
cs_ensayadero_n1_b: A Python pipeline — Demucs for stem separation, Basic Pitch and Omnizart for transcription, Omnizart and madmom for chords — runs on TensorFlow and PyTorch, which is why it ships in the same Docker image as the Next.js server on Railway, behind a job queue that recovers interrupted work on restart.
cs_ensayadero_n2_b: Next.js 16 and React 19 with RLS-aware API routes; Supabase for Postgres, Google OAuth with an allow-list and role claims, and Storage for stems, MIDI and charts. Playback in the browser with Tone.js and wavesurfer.
cs_perico_tagline: A translator with a very specific voice.
cs_perico_intro: Paste ordinary Spanish and it comes back in the voice of Perico Delgado, the Tour winner turned cycling commentator. Live at radioperico.com, with a public course on how it was built.
cs_perico_n1_h: RAG over a corpus of his own words
cs_perico_n1_b: A corpus built from transcribed broadcasts and classified with an LLM, embedded with a multilingual sentence-transformers model and indexed in pgvector on Supabase. Each request retrieves the closest phrases and hands them, as examples to follow, to the Claude API — with the right model for each use case.
cs_perico_n2_b: Python and FastAPI serve the translation as a stream, with embeddings from Hugging Face inference and pooled connections to Postgres; React and Vite on the front, with dictation and speech synthesis. An evaluation suite and spending caps keep it honest.
cs_paellalab_tagline: The arithmetic behind a good rice.
cs_paellalab_intro: Rice and cooking time in; broth, fat, salt and portions out, from how much water each pan actually loses to evaporation. Around the calculator: recipes, a registry of your own pans, a timer and an AI cooking assistant on Llama 3.3. Installable, offline-capable, bilingual.
cs_paellalab_n1_h: A small assistant on cheap inference
cs_paellalab_n1_b: Embeddings from Hugging Face, vector search in Postgres, generation with Llama 3.3 70B on Groq, with rate limiting written into the route itself — a hundred messages a day, ten a minute — sized for roughly fifteen users. A frontier model would have cost more per month than the app is worth, and would not have answered a question about rice any better.
cs_paellalab_n2_b: Only authentication and navigation load eagerly; every landing section waits until it is visible. The gated content exists twice on purpose — enforced on the server, softened on the client with a fade — because the first is the rule and the second is the manners.
cs_paellalab_n3_b: Every pan loses water at its own pace, so each one gets a quick evaporation test. The app turns that measurement into how much broth a given amount of rice needs for the time it will cook, and works out the rest of the quantities from there.
cs_carabanchel_tagline: A neighbourhood, mapped by the people living in it.
cs_carabanchel_intro: An interactive map of the cultural and commercial fabric of Carabanchel, in Madrid, built with the IED: editors publish collections through a CMS and the public app draws them as layers over Mapbox — local commerce, the people who sustain it, and the places at risk of disappearing. Built by two, not solo.
cs_carabanchel_n1_b: Rather than storing loose latitude and longitude columns, a feature's geometry is a dynamic zone built from GeoJSON components. A non-technical editor fills in a form and the API emits a valid FeatureCollection the map consumes directly — plus bulk import for the collections that arrived as files, and regeneration on save.
cs_carabanchel_n2_h: A composed map, and lists that stay smooth
cs_carabanchel_n2_b: Mapbox GL runs under Leaflet rather than standalone, which kept the plugin ecosystem available, and the side panel virtualises its feature list so a collection of hundreds of points scrolls without dropping frames on the phones people actually walk around with.
